title: Sublease Legality & Landlord Disclosure Best Practices
section: Part One · Module 3 - STR Regulations & Compliance

slides.title: A lease that sounds permissive is not written authority for short stays
slides.subtitle: Lesson 3.5. Sublease Legality & Landlord Disclosure Best Practices
meta: Education only. Not legal or insurance advice. Sample clauses need attorney review.
slides.notes:
In lesson 3.4 you scored Alder Street and landed on investigate. Two of the rows on your to-do list were lease rows. This lesson is about fixing those, and about reading any lease with a sharper eye.

By the end you'll be able to read a lease and tell whether it gives you explicit written authority for short stays, or whether it only sounds like it does. That difference is where a lot of arbitrage operators get hurt.

You'll learn the ten topics written consent should cover, what to disclose to the owner, and which questions go to an attorney or an insurer instead of to you. You'll leave with a completed consent review for one lease.

One ground rule before we start. I'll show you sample addendum language later. It's illustrative only. It's not legal advice, and an attorney licensed in the property's state needs to review it before anyone signs.

slides.title: Subletting and short stays are separate questions that need separate answers

left.head: An ordinary sublet
left.note: What most leases and some state laws address
items: You hand possession to one person for a stretch of time
That person lives there and pays you; you pay the landlord
The arrangement has a start date and an end date

right.head: Short-term rental arbitrage
items: You keep control of the unit
A new group of guests arrives every few nights
Alder Street: about 85 stays a year at 3 nights each
Over a 24-month lease, roughly 170 separate guest groups

box.label: The practical rule
box.text: When you read a lease, statute, or landlord email, ask which question it answers. If it only talks about subletting, you still need a separate, explicit answer on short stays.

slides.notes:
Students often treat "Can I sublet?" and "Can I run an Airbnb?" as the same question. They aren't, and mixing them up is how people end up in court.

An ordinary sublet usually means you hand the unit to one person for a stretch of time. They live there, they pay you, you pay the landlord, and it has a start and an end date.

Arbitrage is different in kind. You keep control. A new group arrives every few nights. Alder Street expects about 85 stays a year at an average of 3 nights. Over a 24-month lease, that's roughly 170 separate guest groups. A landlord who agreed to a sublet was probably picturing one subtenant, not 170 check-ins.

So here's the habit I want you to build. Every time you read a lease clause, a statute, or an email from the landlord, ask which of the two questions it answers. If it only answers the sublet question, you still need a separate, explicit answer on short stays.

slides.title: A New York tenant can hold a sublet right and still have no lawful path to short stays
rows: Some tenants in buildings with four or more units may sublease with the landlord's advance written consent, which can't be unreasonably withheld. The notice process is built around a named subtenant and a term.
Whether repeated stays under 30 days are legal
Whether whole-unit stays under 30 days are allowed. For whole units, the answer is no.
Nothing for a whole-unit arbitrage plan

box.label: Confirm with
box.text: An attorney licensed in the property's state: how the lease, state law, and local code classify your plan. A sublet, a license to occupy, or a hotel-type use can trigger different rules.

slides.notes:
New York shows why the two questions split.

Real Property Law section 226-b gives some tenants in buildings with four or more units a right to sublease. The tenant needs the landlord's advance written consent, and the landlord can't unreasonably withhold it. The statute's notice process is built around a named subtenant and a sublease term. What it doesn't do is tell you whether repeated stays under 30 days are legal.

New York City answers that separately, through the Office of Special Enforcement. For whole units, the answer is no.

So a tenant could have a real, statutory sublet right and still have no lawful path to running short stays. The sublet right answers one question. The city rule answers the other.

This is also why the label matters. Depending on the lease, state law, and local code, your plan might be treated as a sublet, a license to occupy, a hotel-type use, or something else. Each label can pull in different rules. That classification is a question for an attorney licensed in the property's state, not for you or me.

slides.title: Written authority has four parts, and missing any one means you don't have it yet

nodes.d: Owner of record, or an agent with written authority. Check the county property record.
Short stays through listed channels. "Residential purposes" doesn't name it.
The exact unit and exact tenant, including your LLC
A signed addendum the lease references, not an email thread

box.label: This fails if
box.text: A leasing agent says "should be fine" with no authority to change the lease. Ask for the management agreement page or a letter showing the agent's authority.

slides.notes:
Written authority has four parts. If any one is missing, you don't have it yet.

First, the right person signs. That's the owner of record or an agent with written authority to bind the owner. A leasing agent who says "should be fine" may have no power to change the lease at all. Check the owner's name against the county property record. If an agent signs, ask for the management agreement page or a letter that shows their authority.

Second, it names the use. The document should say short stays through listed booking channels are allowed. General words like "residential purposes" or "guests permitted" don't name the use.

Third, it names the parties and the unit. The exact unit, the exact tenant, and your LLC if you're signing through one.

Fourth, it's attached to the lease. A signed addendum that the lease references is far stronger than a separate email thread. Lesson 5.3 walks through a full addendum line by line.

slides.title: Landlord consent can't override a city ban, a residence rule, or an HOA restriction
items: Airbnb tells hosts to read the lease, talk to the landlord, and check HOA or co-op rules before hosting ([article 1397](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/1397)).
Some cities make the landlord's written approval part of the permit itself.
Los Angeles requires written landlord approval before a renter can register for home-sharing ([LA FAQ](https://planning.lacity.gov/ordinances/docs/HomeSharing/adopted/faq.pdf)).
The city publishes a [landlord authorization form](https://planning.lacity.gov/odocument/b044ea0f-be5d-4da5-8144-18b0c3fad092/AFFIDAVIT.pdf) for that purpose.
Los Angeles also limits home-sharing to a primary residence, so the form alone doesn't make an arbitrage plan legal there.
slides.notes:
Landlord consent is necessary, but it has limits. It can't override a city ban, a primary-residence rule, or an HOA restriction. The owner can say yes to you and the building or the city can still say no.

Airbnb's own guidance points the same way. It tells hosts to read the lease, talk to the landlord, and check HOA or co-op rules before hosting.

Some cities go further and build the landlord's written approval into the permit itself. Los Angeles requires written landlord approval before a renter can register for home-sharing, and the city publishes a landlord authorization form for exactly that purpose.

But here's the catch in LA. Home-sharing is limited to a primary residence. So even a signed landlord form doesn't make an arbitrage plan legal there, because you don't live in the unit. That's the H2 hard stop from lesson 3.4. Consent is one layer. It doesn't replace the others.

slides.title: Ten topics belong in writing before the first thing goes wrong
rows: Short stays of a stated minimum and maximum length are permitted
Which platforms, and whether direct bookings are allowed
How guests enter and which common areas they may use
Maximum guests per stay, and whether visitors are allowed
Coverage types and limits, who is named, proof on renewal
Who fixes what, response times, who pays, how damage is reported
Quiet hours, trash, parking, smoking, pets
Owner consents to permit applications at the address and signs required forms
Who answers neighbor or owner calls, how fast, day and night
What happens if rules change, how either side ends it, cure periods
slides.notes:
Think of the consent as the operating agreement between you and the owner. If a topic will matter the first time something goes wrong, it belongs in writing now.

Most of these are obvious once you see them. Permitted use removes the "residential only" argument. Booking channels tell the owner where the unit is advertised. Guest access and occupancy head off building disputes and noise worries. Insurance lines the lease up with your actual policy.

Two items surprise people. Item 8 is permit authority. Some cities want the owner's signature or consent on the permit application. You don't want to discover that after you've signed a two-year lease and the owner has gone cold.

Item 10 is change in law and exit. It protects you as much as the owner. If a new ordinance bans your use, you want a clean way to convert to a standard tenancy or end the lease. The alternative is a default.

We'll fill all ten for Alder Street in a few slides.

slides.title: Disclose five things in plain words so the consent covers what you'll actually run
rows: You lease the unit and host paying guests for a few nights at a time through named platforms. Alder Street: about 85 stays a year, roughly 1.6 check-ins a week.
Who cleans, who handles maintenance, who responds in person. Not hired yet? Say so and send a name before the first booking.
What you check and what house rules guests accept. Airbnb bans open-invite parties ([article 3345](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/3345)), but your own rules still need writing.
Your STR insurance, deposit or damage process, and reporting. Host damage protection isn't insurance ([article 3733](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/3733)).
How neighbors reach you, quiet hours, how complaints are handled ([article 1397](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/1397))

box.label: Put it on one page
box.text: Attach a one-page operating summary to the addendum. Keep every document in one dated folder.

slides.notes:
The owner should understand exactly what business will run in their property. That's fair to them, and it protects you. A consent obtained with a vague description can be attacked later as consent to something else.

Disclose five things. The operating model, with the expected volume. For Alder Street that's about 85 stays a year, roughly 1.6 check-ins a week. The local team: who cleans, who fixes, who shows up. Your guest screening. Airbnb says it doesn't allow open-invite parties and may block higher-risk reservations, but that's a platform policy. Your own rules still need to be written down.

Then damage handling. Be accurate here. Airbnb states that Host damage protection isn't an insurance policy, so don't describe it to an owner as insurance. And neighbors: how they reach you and what quiet hours apply.

Put all five on one page and attach it to the addendum. If the owner later says "I didn't know it would be this many guests," you point to a page they signed. Then keep everything in one dated folder. That folder is what an attorney, insurer, or permit office will ask for.

slides.title: Most arbitrage clauses sound permissive but give you nothing until someone signs
rows: "Tenant may not sublet or assign without Landlord's prior written consent."
Nothing until the landlord signs a consent that names short stays
Usually social guests, not paying ones
"Premises shall be used for residential purposes only."
Text message: "Airbnb is fine with me."
Unsigned, unattached, no terms, maybe from someone without authority
"Landlord consents to Tenant's use of the Premises for short-term rentals."
The use, but silent on channels, occupancy, insurance, permits, and exit
A signed addendum covering all ten topics
Explicit authority with terms both sides can follow
slides.notes:
This is where most arbitrage leases go wrong. The words sound permissive, but they don't say what you need.

The standard sublet clause says you need the landlord's prior written consent. People read that as "ask and you'll get it." It actually gives you nothing until the landlord signs something that names short stays.

"Tenant may have guests" usually means social guests, not paying ones. "Residential purposes only" can be read to exclude a lodging business. And a text saying "Airbnb is fine with me" is unsigned, unattached, has no terms, and may come from someone with no authority.

The row I want you to notice is the medium-risk one. A one-line consent to short-term rentals is a big step up from silence. But the first time a neighbor complains about six guests, you and the owner will be arguing about terms that were never written. Occupancy, channels, insurance, permits, exit: none of it is there.

The lower-risk row is a signed addendum covering all ten topics. Even that stays subject to local law.

slides.title: An explicit addendum puts compliance on you and plans for the day the rules change
items: **1. Permitted use.** Furnished stays of fewer than 30 nights by paying guests, for the full term and any renewal.
**3. Occupancy and access.** No more than 5 overnight guests. Keypad entry, shared laundry, one assigned rear parking space.
**4. Compliance.** Tenant obtains every permit and tax account. Landlord signs any required owner form within 10 business days.
**8. Change in law.** If short stays become prohibited, either party may give 30 days' notice to convert to a standard tenancy or end without penalty.
**9. Breach and cure.** Written notice of a breach, then [number] days to cure before consent can be revoked.

box.label: Illustrative language only
box.text: Excerpts only. Not legal advice. An attorney licensed in the property's state reviews it before anyone signs.

slides.notes:
The lesson includes a full ten-clause sample addendum. Here are the five clauses I want you to understand first.

Clause 1 names the use: furnished stays of fewer than 30 nights by paying guests, for the whole term and any renewal. Clause 3 sets occupancy and access for this unit: no more than 5 guests, keypad entry, the shared laundry, and one rear parking space.

Clause 4 matters most. It puts compliance on you. You get and keep every permit and tax account. The landlord agrees to sign any owner form the city requires within 10 business days.

Clause 8 plans for a change in law. If short stays become prohibited, either side can give 30 days' notice to convert to a standard tenancy or end the lease without penalty. Clause 9 is breach and cure.

Notice what this language doesn't do. It doesn't promise the use is legal. And whether clauses 8 and 9 are enforceable as written depends on state law. That's the attorney's job, and you should ask specifically how they interact with local tenant protections.

slides.title: Alder Street's three documents give you a restriction, a risk, and a friendly text
rows: "Tenant shall not sublet any part of the Premises or assign this Lease without Landlord's written consent."
Silent on short stays. At best, consent is possible. You need a signed addendum.
"Either party may terminate this Lease upon 60 days' written notice."
The L1 flag from 3.4. Ask for breach and cure, and that clause 14 doesn't apply while the addendum is in force.
"I'm ok with the Airbnb thing as long as there are no problems."
Unsigned, no terms, "problems" undefined. Save it as good faith and use it to open the addendum talk.
slides.notes:
Back to Unit 4B, 218 Alder Street. The landlord owns the four-unit building and offered a 24-month lease at $1,950 a month. You labeled it investigate in 3.4, with L1 and L2 on the list. Now you look at the actual documents. I'm assuming you have three.

Item A is clause 9 of the standard lease. It restricts subletting and asks for written consent. It doesn't mention short stays at all. As written it gives you nothing. At best it tells you consent is possible.

Item B is clause 14, and it's the L1 flag. Either party can end the lease on 60 days' written notice. We'll put a number on that risk on the next slide.

Item C is a text from the landlord: "I'm ok with the Airbnb thing as long as there are no problems." It's friendly, and it's weak. It's unsigned, it has no terms, and who decides what a problem is? Save it as evidence of good faith. Use it to open the addendum conversation. Don't rely on it.

slides.title: A notice at month 4 could leave about $5,942 of Alder Street's setup unrecovered
slides.side:
The landlord gives 60 days' notice at the end of month 4, so the lease ends after month 6.

In the stress case, at $129 a month, you'd have recovered only **$774** by month 6.

side_box.label: What to ask for
side_box.text: Clause 9 of the illustrative addendum (breach and cure), plus a statement that clause 14 doesn't apply while the addendum is in force.

slides.notes:
Let's put a number on Item B.

Your sunk setup cost is $12,050. At the base-case net of $1,018 a month, payback takes 11.8 months. Now suppose the landlord gives 60 days' notice at the end of month 4. The lease ends after month 6.

By then you'd have earned back about $6,108, which is $1,018 times 6. That leaves about $5,942 of setup cost unrecovered. And that's the good case. In the stress case, at $129 a month, you'd have recovered only $774 by month 6.

That's why a no-cause termination clause scores a 2 on the 3.4 scorecard. It's the clause that turns your furniture budget into the landlord's option.

So here's the ask. Request clause 9 from the illustrative addendum, breach and cure, in place of no-cause termination. And ask for a plain statement that clause 14 doesn't apply while the addendum is in force. Then have your attorney confirm the result is enforceable in your state.

slides.title: Alder Street's addendum fills all ten topics with the unit's own facts
rows: Keypad lock on 4B; shared laundry; one rear parking space
STR liability policy quoted at $1,300 a year (canonical); declarations page to landlord
Tenant pays guest-caused damage; building issues reported within 24 hours
Quiet hours, trash day, no smoking in house rules
Landlord signs any owner form; permit costs $250 a year (canonical)
Name and 24-hour number delivered before first stay
Convert or end on 30 days' notice; 30-day cure period (assumption)
slides.notes:
Now build the addendum around the ten topics, using Alder Street's facts.

Permitted use is stays under 30 nights for the full 24-month term. Channels are Airbnb, Vrbo, and a direct website. Guests get in through a keypad lock on 4B and can use the shared laundry and one rear parking space. Occupancy is capped at 5, because the unit sleeps 5.

Insurance is the STR liability policy quoted at $1,300 a year, and the landlord gets the declarations page. You pay for guest-caused damage and report building issues within 24 hours. Quiet hours, trash day, and no smoking go into the house rules.

Permit authority: the landlord signs any owner form, and the permit costs $250 a year. The local contact name and 24-hour number are delivered before the first stay.

The last row is change in law and exit: convert or end on 30 days' notice, with a 30-day cure period. That cure period is an assumption for this example. Your attorney sets the real one.

slides.title: A signed addendum plus a one-page summary clears L2, and breach and cure clears L1

left.head: Operating summary attached
items: About 85 stays a year, average 3 nights
Maximum 5 guests
A named cleaner and a named on-call vendor
Your 24-hour number

right.head: Effect on the 3.4 scorecard
items: L2 guest rights drops from 1 to 0 with a signed addendum covering these rows
L1 termination drops from 2 to 0 if the landlord accepts breach and cure in place of no-cause termination
Item C stays in the folder as good faith, not as permission

slides.notes:
Then attach the operating summary. For Alder Street it's short: about 85 stays a year, an average of 3 nights, a maximum of 5 guests, a named cleaner, a named on-call vendor, and your 24-hour number. One page. The landlord signs it with the addendum.

Now go back to the scorecard from lesson 3.4. With a signed addendum covering these rows, L2, guest rights, drops from 1 to 0. If the landlord accepts breach and cure in place of no-cause termination, L1 drops from 2 to 0. Those were the two lease rows that held Alder Street at investigate.

The landlord's text doesn't disappear. It goes in the folder as evidence the conversation started in good faith. It just isn't what you rely on.

If the landlord won't sign, you're back to H5 in lesson 3.4: no explicit written permission. That's a reject, however friendly the texts are.

slides.title: Confirm who owns the unit and who signs before you review a single clause
slides.text: Part A of the consent review. Save the evidence for every answer with a file name and date.
rows: Owner of record per county property record
Person who will sign, and their role
If an agent signs, document showing their authority
Tenant name exactly as it will appear (you or your LLC)

box.label: Part B, next
box.text: Quote each lease clause or message. Mark which question it answers (sublet, short stays, or neither), its risk (high, medium, lower), and the fix you'll request.

slides.notes:
Your exercise is a consent review on the lease for one address you're considering. Fill in every row before you sign anything.

Part A is authority, and I put it first on purpose. Look up the owner of record in the county property record. Write down who will actually sign and what their role is. If an agent is signing, get the document that shows their authority. And write the tenant name exactly as it'll appear on the lease, whether that's you or your LLC.

For every answer, save the evidence with a file name and date. This is the same folder habit from the disclosure section.

Part B is the clause review. Quote each clause or message word for word. Then ask which question it answers: sublet, short stays, or neither. Rate the risk as high, medium, or lower, using the clause table we went through. Then write the fix you'll ask for. For Alder Street, clause 14 would be high risk with a request for breach and cure.

slides.title: Check all ten topics against the signed document, clause by clause
slides.notes:
Part C is the ten-topic coverage check. For each topic, mark whether a signed document covers it, write the clause number, and note anything still needed. If a topic lives only in an email, it's a no.

Part D in the lesson is the disclosure summary. Check off the operating model and stays per year, the local team names, guest screening rules, damage handling and insurance, and the neighbor contact plan. Record the date you sent it and whether the owner acknowledged it.

Then make the decision at the bottom. Do you have explicit written authority in hand, yes or no? If no, list what's missing, who will provide it, and by what date.

A no here has a hard consequence. You don't accept guests. It also sends you back to the 3.4 scorecard to update L1 through L4 with what you learned. That's the loop: score, review, fix, rescore.

slides.title: Four people confirm what the lease and the landlord can't settle alone
rows: Attorney licensed in the property's state
Whether the lease and addendum give explicit authority for short stays; any state sublet statute; whether termination, cure, and change-in-law terms are enforceable
Whether the permit requires the owner's signature or a landlord authorization form, and whether a renter can hold the permit at all
The policy covers the disclosed operation, and whether the landlord can be named as an additional insured
HOA, condo board, or building manager (if any)
Building rules don't restrict short stays, regardless of the landlord's consent
slides.notes:
Four people confirm the parts of this that neither you nor the landlord can settle alone.

An attorney licensed in the property's state confirms whether the lease and addendum actually give you explicit authority for short stays. They also check any state sublet statute, like the New York one, and whether the termination, cure, and change-in-law terms will hold up.

The local licensing or planning office confirms whether the permit needs the owner's signature or a landlord authorization form. Ask the blunt question too: can a renter hold this permit at all?

Your insurance broker confirms that the policy covers the operation you disclosed. That's another reason the operating summary matters. The broker should see the same description the landlord signed. Ask whether the landlord can be named as an additional insured.

And if there's an HOA, condo board, or building manager, they confirm the building rules don't restrict short stays. The landlord's consent doesn't override them.

slides.title: Review one lease for written authority this week
items: Look up the owner of record on the county property site and compare it with the person who will sign.
Quote every sublet, use, guest, and termination clause in the draft lease and mark which question each answers.
Draft a one-page operating summary: stays per year, maximum guests, local team, 24-hour number.
Mark which of the ten topics are covered in writing and list what's still needed.
slides.next: Next: Sam's 4.1, How to Find a Money-Making Market - 2026 Method. Watch the comparable-revenue and supply checks that clear C3 and C8. Lesson 5.3, Sublease Addendum Deep Dive, drafts the addendum clause by clause.
slides.notes:
Four things for this week, each under an hour.

Look up the owner of record on the county property site. Compare it with the person who'll sign. If they don't match, find out why before anything else.

Go through the draft lease and quote every clause about subletting, use, guests, and termination. Next to each, write which question it answers: sublet, short stays, or neither.

Draft your one-page operating summary. Stays per year, maximum guests, who's on your local team, and your 24-hour number.

Then run the ten topics and mark which are covered in writing and which are still missing.

Module 4 moves from permission to market evidence. Sam's 4.1, How to Find a Money-Making Market, starts the live research. Watch for the comparable-revenue and supply checks, because they clear rows C3 and C8 on your 3.4 scorecard. When you're ready to draft the actual document, lesson 5.3, Sublease Addendum Deep Dive, walks through it clause by clause. Bring your consent review worksheet to both.

slides.title: The rules behind this lesson come from statute, city pages, and Airbnb's own help center

items.note: The city's landlord authorization form exists

slides.notes:
Here are the primary sources behind this lesson, all checked on 25 September 2026.

The New York sublet right comes from the state's Real Property Law, section 226-b, on the state senate's legislation site. The 30-day whole-unit rule and the lease certification come from New York City's Office of Special Enforcement.

The Los Angeles points come from City Planning: the FAQ for written landlord approval and the primary-residence rule, and the landlord authorization form itself. I'll be straight about that last one. It was confirmed from the official search listing. I haven't walked through the form's contents here, so open it yourself if you're working in LA.

The three Airbnb help articles support the lease and HOA check, the neighbor conversation, the party policy, and the point that Host damage protection isn't insurance.

The Alder Street figures come from the canonical example set. Rules change, so recheck each page before you rely on it for a real lease.
